title: Introduction to the command line

The shell


The terminal is the window; the shell is the program inside it that reads your commands.
We use Bash, the shell on most Linux servers. macOS uses zsh by default, which works almost the same.

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
Bioinformaticians use it


Almost all servers and clusters run Linux, and you reach them only through a shell.
Most bioinformatics tools have no graphical interface: they are commands.
Files are huge: you cannot open a 10 GB FASTQ file in a word processor.
Commands can be saved in scripts: your analysis becomes repeatable and documented.

Relative path: starts where you are. .. is the folder above, . is the folder you are in.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
section: Where we are in the workflow
text: Where we are in the workflow

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
From plant to reads

Plant tissue → DNA extraction → Library preparation → Sequencing → FASTQ files

Each step can introduce technical effects that later show up in QC reports.

We sequence to answer a biological question: which variants, which alleles, which genes are expressed.
All of these assume that the sequencing data reflects the real biology of the plant. QC checks whether that assumption is reasonable.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
What can go wrong?



Technical issue

Biological consequence




Low base quality
→
False SNPs


Adapter contamination
→
Artificial variants


GC bias
→
Skewed allele frequencies


High duplication
→
Overconfidence in genotypes







In a breeding context this could mean choosing the wrong markers, missing true marker-trait associations, misjudging genetic diversity.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Step 1: DNA extraction





Polyphenols and polysaccharides interfere with enzymes and make DNA sticky
DNA quality varies between samples, tissues, methods and people

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Step 2: Library preparation





DNA is sheared, adapters are ligated, fragments are amplified by PCR
Degraded DNA gives uneven coverage
PCR amplifies some fragments more than others: PCR bias

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Step 3: Sequencing





Base calls get less accurate towards the end of the read
Errors accumulate over cycles
Lanes and runs differ in quality

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Plant genomes are special
QC tools are generic. They don’t know your data comes from a plant.

Large genomes, high repeat content
Polyploidy and high heterozygosity
GC content that varies between species


So GC plots can look unusual and duplication can be high, even for good data.
QC tools show you what looks unusual. You need biological knowledge to decide why.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
What FastQC does

Reads a FASTQ file: millions of reads, each with a quality score per base
Runs a series of standard tests, called modules
Writes an HTML report with a figure or table per module


FastQC does not know your experiment or your plans. The interpretation and decisions are up to you.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Pass, warn, fail
Every module gets a label: ✅ pass, ⚠️ warn, ❌ fail.

A fail does not mean the data is unusable
A pass does not mean the data is perfect
Thresholds are generic: they assume random, whole-genome DNA


Treat the flags as signals to investigate, not as decisions.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Basic statistics




Shows file name, number of reads, read length, GC %.
Check you are looking at the right sample, and compare read numbers between files.
Never raises a warning.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per base sequence quality




Shows quality scores at each position in the read.
We expect high quality at the start, a slow decline towards the end.
Warning signs include a sharp drop, large parts of the read in the red, big differences between samples.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Your turn: Pause the video





From which position does the quality drop?
Would you use these reads as they are?

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
The answer





The median (red line) stays above 26, but the mean (blue line) drops below 28 around position 19. From position 26 at least a quarter of the reads are in the red zone.
Not as they are. Trim the low-quality ends, then run FastQC again.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per sequence quality scores




Shows the mean quality per read, not per position.
We expect one sharp peak at high quality.
Warning signals include a large share of low-quality reads, or a second peak. Points to library or sequencing problems, or poor starting material.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per base sequence content




Shows the share of A, C, G and T at each position.
We expect flat lines for random genomic DNA.
But many library types are biased at the start of the read, RNA-seq always. Ask whether the pattern is expected for your experiment.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per sequence GC content




It shows GC content of the reads, against a theoretical curve.
We expect roughly a normal distribution, peaking at the genome’s GC content.
Warning signals include a second peak or a shifted sample: contamination. In plants also repeats or genome composition. Always compare samples with each other.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
N content and read length








N content: the sequencer could not call the base. A few at the end of reads is normal.
Read lenght: Illumina reads have one length; PacBio and Nanopore vary. After trimming, lengths vary too.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Sequence duplication levels




It shows how often identical sequences occur.
We expect most sequences to occur once in a diverse library.
High duplication comes from PCR bias, low library complexity or very deep sequencing. In plants also conserved and repetitive regions. Normal in RNA-seq.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Overrepresented sequences and adapters








Overrepresented means single sequences are much more common than expected. Could be adapters, primers, repeats, or real biology.
Adapter content shows which adapter is present, and how much. Tells you what to trim.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
K-mer content (optional)




A k-mer is a short sequence of length k, for example the 7-mer ATCGTGA.
FastQC looks for k-mers enriched at certain positions. Enrichment at the start or end of reads usually means adapters, primers or library artefacts.
Only 2 % of the reads are checked.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Three possible outcomes

QC helps you to decide what to do next with your data.


Use as is: minor or expected warnings




Process: trim adapters or low-quality ends, then run FastQC again




Investigate: serious problems may mean re-preparing, resequencing or excluding the sample

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
QC in a reproducible workflow


Run QC the same way on all samples
Record which issues you saw
Document what you did about them, and why

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Many samples: MultiQC

Dozens of samples × 2 reads × FastQC before and after trimming: too many reports to read one by one.

MultiQC collects them into one report:

Samples side by side
Outliers stand out
Systematic problems across samples become visible


You will use FastQC, MultiQC and fastp in the exercises.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Summary

QC protects your biological conclusions from technical problems
Remeber problems can start long before the FASTQ file: during extraction, library preparation, sequencing
FastQC flags are signals, not verdicts; interpret them for your data and organism
After QC: use, trim and re-check, or investigate
Document what you checked and what you did



FastQC figures and module descriptions adapted from the FastQC documentation, Babraham Bioinformatics.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
text: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) turns DNA or RNA from a sample into millions of short text strings, the so called reads. Reads contain the called bases, but on their own tell you very little. Before they can answer a biological question, we need to check that they are trustworthy (are of good enough quality), and work out where in the genome each one comes from. This is the basis of many different workflows, regardless of what data you will work with. So that is what we will concentrate on in this module.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
section: The data before it reaches us
text:
The data before it reaches us
Before any NGS data hits a terminal, it’s journey typically begins in the minds of the researchers, and then goes to the lab:

Study design: what is the question the experiment should answer? which samples are necessary? how many replicates should be included?
Sample extraction: Samples are taken, and DNA or RNA is extracted. Its purity and integrity limit everything that follows.
Library preparation: the DNA or RNA is fragmented, adapters and sample indexes are added so the sequencer can process the samples.
Sequencing: the sequencer reads the fragments and writes the results to so called FASTQ files: they contain the sequence of each read, as well as a quality score for every base of the sequence.

Often, you will get FASTQ files from a sequencing facility without having seen any of the steps above. However, each of them can leave traces in the data, and can influence the answers you will get from the data. This is why quality control is so importan: it can tell you much about your data, and the answers you can get from them.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
text:
Day 1: Quality control
What we do: We will check the quality of the raw cassava reads with FastQC, collect the reports with MultiQC, trim the reads with fastp, and check them again.
Why is it important? Bad input gives bad results, and you need to know your data to assess if you can trust its results. Your analyses will run whether the input data is good or bad, it is up to you to interpret them. Low-quality bases can look like mutations, leftover adapters stop reads from mapping, and a contaminated sample can look like a biological difference. Quality control tells you whether the data can be used as it is, needs cleaning, or should not be used at all.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
text:
Day 2: Mapping
What we do: We will map our quality controlled reads to the cassava reference genome using specialized programs: DNA reads will be mapped with Bowtie 2, and RNA-seq reads with STAR. This results in a BAM file, which we can inspect with samtools.
Why is it important? A read is only useful once you know where in the genome it belongs. Mapping places each read on the reference genome. With this information we can run many more analyses: getting information on the gene function, finding variants, counting reads per gene, or measuring coverage.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
section: The data after we are done with it
text:
The data after we are done with it
In other modules of this course you will encounter some analyses that come after the quality control and mapping: you will encounter genome annotation (what do we know about the locations we mapped the reads to?), RNAseq analyses (what genes are expressed in our samples?), and metagenomics (how can we deal with mixed species samples, and what information can we get out of them?).

title: Mapping sequencing reads
text:
Bowtie 2
Now we are all set to map our paired end DNA sequences onto the reference.
Bowtie2 is an ultrafast and memory-efficient tool for aligning sequencing reads to long reference sequences. It is particularly good at aligning reads of about 50 up to 100s or 1,000s of characters, and particularly good at aligning to relatively long (e.g. mammalian) genomes. Bowtie 2 indexes the genome with an FM Index to keep its memory footprint small: for the human genome, its memory footprint is typically around 3.2 GB. Bowtie 2 supports gapped, local, and paired-end alignment modes.

title: Mapping sequencing reads
text:
Create index
Each NGS mapper uses indices to accelerate the mapping process, but unfortunately each one has his own way to create these indices. Therefore we first need to create the index for bowtie2 of our reference sequence, which we will call Bowtie2Cassava01Index and will be located in the reference directory.
Create a bash file within the scripts directory:
touch bowtie_index.sh
And copy the following into the file:
#! /bin/bash -l

#SBATCH -A <course project ID>
#SBATCH -t 05:00
#SBATCH -n 1

set -ueo pipefail

# Define input reference and output directory
REFERENCE=mapping/ref/chromosome01.fasta
OUTPUT_DIR=mapping/ref/

apptainer exec singularity_images/bowtie2_2.5.5.sif \
    bowtie2-build -o 3 $REFERENCE $OUTPUT_DIR/Bowtie2Cassava01Index
    
echo "complete"
Save the above code and run the script using
sbatch scripts/bowtie_index.sh

title: Mapping sequencing reads
text:
Map with bowtie2
Now that we have the index we create a directory for the bowtie2 results:
mkdir mapping/bowtie2
and then we can run the mapping:
Make a file in the scripts folder bowtie2_mapping.sh.
#! /bin/bash -l

#SBATCH -A <course project ID>
#SBATCH -t 15:00
#SBATCH -n 4

set -ueo pipefail

# Get CPUS allocated to slurm script (-n above)
CPUS=$SLURM_NPROCS

INDEX=mapping/ref/Bowtie2Cassava01Index
R1=raw/TMEB117_R1_frac.fastq
R2=raw/TMEB117_R2_frac.fastq

# trimmed data 
# R1=fastp/TMEB117_fastp-trimmed_R1.fastq
# R2=fastp/TMEB117_fastp-trimmed_R2.fastq

apptainer exec singularity_images/bowtie2_2.5.5.sif \
    bowtie2 --very-sensitive-local \
    --threads $CPUS \
    -x $INDEX \
    -S mapping/bowtie2/TMEB117.sam \
    -1 $R1 \
    -2 $R2 |& tee mapping/bowtie2/TMEB117.log

echo "complete"

#SBATCH -t 15:00
#SBATCH -n 4

Why not just search?


20 million read pairs × a genome of roughly 700 Mb (cassava)
Comparing every read with every position: about 1016 comparisons
Searching with BLAST would take weeks


Mappers first build an index of the reference, once. Then each read is looked up in the index, like a word in the index at the back of a book.

What an alignment allows








Difference
Why it happens




Mismatch
Sequencing error, or a real variant (SNP)


Insertion / deletion
Sequencing error (homopolymers), or a real indel


Soft clipping
Adapter left on the read, low-quality ends, structural variant




Every difference costs points. The mapper reports the alignment with the best score.

title: Mapping sequencing reads
text:
End-to-end or local?

End-to-end: the whole read must align. Unaligned ends are penalised as mismatches.
Local: the ends may be clipped if they don’t fit. Good when reads still carry adapter or low-quality ends.


In Bowtie 2: --very-sensitive (end-to-end) vs --very-sensitive-local (local). You will try both.

Reads that fit in many places
Genomes are full of repeats: transposons, gene families, duplicated regions.







A read that fits equally well in several places is a multi-mapping read. The mapper picks one at random, or reports all of them.
MAPQ (mapping quality) says how sure the mapper is: 0 means it could be anywhere.

Plant genomes are special


Large and full of transposable elements: often more than half the genome
Often polyploid: several copies of each chromosome, similar but not identical
Often heterozygous: cassava is, so the two copies of a chromosome differ


Your cultivar is not the reference cultivar. Differences between them will look like mismatches to the mapper.

In RNA-seq, reads come from spliced transcripts. Many reads span an exon-exon junction.

STAR, HISAT2: allow a read to be split across an intron
An annotation (GTF) tells them where known exons and junctions are
They also find new junctions from the data


That is why STAR needs the .gtf file when it builds its index, and Bowtie 2 doesn’t.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
What are containers?
Containers are stand-alone pieces of software that require a container management tool to run. They are build and exchanged as container images that specify the contents of the container, such as the operating system, all dependencies, and software in an isolated environment. The container management tool then takes the images and build the container. These management tools can be run on all operating systems, and since the container has the operating system within it, it will run the same in all environments. Container images are easily portable and immutable, so they are stable over time.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Running Containers
There are several programs that can be used to build and run containers. Docker, Apptainer, and Podman are the most commonly used platforms to date. They all have their pros and cons. If you are using a Windows machine that only you are using, then Docker is likely the least complex tool to install. On multi-user systems like a server, Apptainer is the best tool for the job. For this tutorial and the rest of the course, we will use Apptainer commands.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Getting apptainer image
One good place to get quality controlled Apptainer/Singularity containers that contain the tools we want to use is seqera containers.

Open their homepage in a new tab.
In the searchbar, type in the tool you want - fastqc




Add the tool you want to have in your container (in this case fastqc from Bioconda). Be aware, the screenshot in this material might show a different tool version than the one you will see.

Click “get container”.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Download container images
To have a nice and clean project directory we will make a new sub-directory that will contain all the singularity images we will use during this tutorial.
mkdir singularity_images
cd singularity_images
Now we can pull the container image from its location into our folder:
apptainer pull --name fastqc_0.13.0.sif oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.13.0--918df8ee88833f73
In this command we tell apptainer, the container system software, to pull a container with a name we can set ourselves, from a source oras....
Then we move out of the directory again:
cd .. 

Running Containers
Once you have pulled the container image, you want to be able to use it. Apptainer can be used to build the container from the image.

running “from the outside”
There are 2 different ways to use a container: run and exec. The apptainer run command launches the container and first runs the %runscript for the container if one is defined, and then runs your command (we will cover %runscript in the Building Containers section). The apptainer exec command will not run the %runscript even if one is defined. It is a small, fiddly detail that might be applicable if you use other people’s containers. After calling Apptainer and the run or exec commands, you can use your software as you usually would
apptainer exec singularity_images/fastqc_0.13.0.sif fastqc --version
This command runs your fastqc_0.13.0.sif container from the image, calls on the program fastqc that is within the container, and shows you the version. If you had installed FastQC locally, you would have just used
fastqc --version






Important



FastQC is just an example. If you want to run any other tool everything after apptainer run or apptainer exec has to be substituted by the name of the specific container image and the run commands for that particular tool!




running interactively “from the inside”
You can also enter the container, and work interactively from within. For that you use the apptainer shell command:
apptainer shell singularity_images/fastqc_0.13.0.sif
Inside the container, your prompt will change to Singularity (remember, that is the legacy name for Apptainer). Now you can use the tools inside the container.
To exit the container, simply type and enter exit.
Great, now we have FastQC ready and can use it. How can we submit the job to the server?

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
SLURM
HPC2N is running SLURM (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) as its job scheduling system. When you submit a job on the cluster log-in node, SLURM will start, execute and monitor your jobs on the working nodes. It allocates access to the cluster resources, and manages the queue of pending jobs. Here is a more thorough documentation of SLURM on Kebnekaise.
To be able to do so, SLURM needs a bit of information from us when we submit a job:

-A: project_ID (to deduct the used computing time from the correct project)
-t allocated time dd-hh:mm:ss (to optimize the job queue)
-n number of cores (default is one)

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Running fastqc with sbatch
We will now write a script that runs fastqc on our samples - using the container we pulled. We will add the slurm flags from above and then submit to the server queue with the SLURM command sbatch.
Again, we want to maintain a clean and orderly project directory:
In your NGS_course folder, create a directory for the FastQC output and a new directory called scripts. Within the scripts directory create a file called fastqc.sh.
mkdir fastqc
mkdir scripts
cd scripts
touch fastqc.sh






TipTouch



Touch makes a new file with the given name. You can then open it in the file explorer (left side of VS-Code).


Copy the following into the file, and save the contents. Read through the file and try to understand what the different lines are doing.
#! /bin/bash -l
# The name of the compute account you are running in, mandatory.
#SBATCH -A <course project ID>
# Request runtime for the job (HHH:MM:SS) where 168 hours is the maximum. Here asking for 15 min. 
#SBATCH -t 15:00
# Request resources - here for four cpus
#SBATCH -n 4

# FastQC needs the output folder to exist
mkdir -p fastqc

apptainer exec singularity_images/fastqc_0.13.0.sif \
    fastqc -t 4 --outdir fastqc/ raw/*.fastq
echo "complete"
The slurm options used here:

A: project ID (you find it in Canvas)
t allocated time dd-hh:mm:ss
n number of cpus

FastQC’s -t 4 tells it to use the four cpus we asked for.
Move back into the NGS_course directory and submit the script to slurm:
cd ..
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh
After running a bash script you will get a slurm output. Look at that output. See if you understand what that output contains.
less slurm-XXXXX.out
Locate the output of FastQC.






Note



Which output directory did you specify in the batch file?

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Welcome
High-throughput sequencing: from the molecule to the reads.

With slides based on presentations of Nicolas Delhomme and Prof. Nathaniel Street


Welcome. This lecture covers how DNA and RNA are turned into sequence data: where the technology came from, how libraries are made, how the main short- and long-read platforms work, and what kinds of errors each one makes. That last part leads straight into the quality control lecture and today’s exercises.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: Deciphering the blueprint of an organism
text:
Deciphering the blueprint of an organism

1977: Sanger’s chain-termination method, one fragment per reaction
2001: first draft human genome (Human Genome Project and Celera). Full project ran 1990–2003: ~13 years, ~$2.7 billion
2022: first complete human genome (T2T-CHM13, gapless except chrY), made with long reads
Today: a few hundred dollars in reagents and a 1–2 day run


Lander et al. 2001 Nature 409:860; Venter et al. 2001 Science 291:1304; Nurk et al. 2022 Science 376:44; genome.gov HGP cost fact sheet; Shendure et al. 2017 Nature 550:345


DNA sequencing is not new: Sanger published chain termination in 1977. It went big with the Human Genome Project and Celera, whose drafts appeared together in February 2001 on the covers of Nature and Science. The whole public project, from 1990 to 2003, took about 13 years and about 2.7 billion dollars; the 2001 draft alone cost roughly 300 million. The first complete human genome, gapless except for the Y chromosome, only came in 2022 from the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium, using long reads and a haploid cell line. Today the reagents for a human genome cost a few hundred dollars, and the sequencing run takes one to two days.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
This lecture

Sanger sequencing: the beginning
Library preparation: DNA and RNA
Short reads: Illumina and competitors
Long reads: PacBio and Oxford Nanopore
Choosing a platform: errors, what’s new, NGI


Here is the plan. Many of the following slides are adapted from material by Nathaniel Street at Umeå University, updated for 2026. We start with Sanger sequencing, then how DNA and RNA are prepared, then short-read and long-read platforms, and we finish with how to choose a platform and what errors to expect.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Sanger sequencing: how it started





One reaction per DNA fragment
Genomes needed clone libraries: lots of lab work, lots of chances for mistakes
Low throughput: one read (700–1000 bases) per capillary, 96 capillaries per run
Still used today to check single loci, clones and PCR products



In the Sanger era every read needed its own reaction. To sequence a genome, DNA was fragmented, cloned into vectors, grown in bacteria, purified and sequenced clone by clone, then assembled. That is a lot of lab work and a lot of chances to make mistakes. A capillary instrument such as the ABI 3730xl reads 96 samples per run, so throughput was low.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Chain termination


The reaction contains normal nucleotides plus a small amount of dye-labelled dideoxynucleotides. A ddNTP has no 3’ hydroxyl group, so when the polymerase adds one, the strand stops. Each copy stops at a random position, and its last base carries a colour. Separating the copies by size in a capillary and reading the colours in order gives the sequence.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Reading a Sanger trace



Then: radioactive slab gels, one lane per base, read by eye
Now: four dyes in one capillary, read by a laser
Two overlapping peaks of about half height = a heterozygous position



Early Sanger sequencing used radioactive slab gels with four lanes, one per base, read by eye from an autoradiograph. Capillary instruments with four dyes replaced them. In a chromatogram, a heterozygous position shows a second peak under the main one. In a clean heterozygote the two peaks are about half height each; uneven peaks need a second look. Sanger still serves as the check for single variants found by NGS.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
“Next” (2nd) generation sequencing



Sequencing-by-synthesis: massively parallel sequencing
Millions to billions of fragments sequenced at once
Illumina still dominates, but there is real competition again: Element AVITI, Ultima UG 100/200, MGI / Complete Genomics DNBSEQ, Roche SBX
Gone: Roche 454, SOLiD, Helicos. Ion Torrent: clinical niche





Second-generation sequencing reads millions to billions of DNA fragments at the same time, using sequencing by synthesis. For about ten years Illumina dominated short-read sequencing. That is changing: Element Biosciences, Ultima Genomics, MGI and Complete Genomics, and since June 2026 Roche, whose SBX instrument reads an expanded copy of the DNA through a nanopore, are competing. 454, SOLiD and Helicos are gone; Ion Torrent survives in clinical panels. The timeline also shows the long-read platforms, which we cover later.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
The $1000 genome


Data: NHGRI via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0). 2024–2026: manufacturer claims. Figure: own work, CC BY 4.0


This is the NHGRI cost per human genome, on a log scale. Until 2007 cost fell roughly with Moore’s law, which NHGRI takes as a halving every two years; the Stephens figure on the next slide uses 18 months. When second-generation instruments arrived around 2008, it dropped far faster. The latest NHGRI data point is from 2022, at about 500 dollars. The shaded box shows what manufacturers claim today, 80 to 500 dollars per genome; these are claims, not independent data, and they leave out labour and analysis.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: Sequencing capacity grows faster than Moore’s law
text:
Sequencing capacity grows faster than Moore’s law






Computing power per dollar has kept roughly doubling every two years
Sequencing got cheaper, but computers do not keep up: storing and analysing the data becomes as hard as producing it
2015 projection: 100 million to 2 billion genomes by 2025. Reality: a few million

First human genome: 13 years. SciLifeLab 2016: 1 h



Stephens ZD et al. (2015) Big Data: Astronomical or Genomical? PLoS Biol 13:e1002195 (CC BY 4.0)


Stephens and colleagues compared genomics with other big-data fields in 2015. Their 2015 projection was that between 100 million and 2 billion human genomes could be sequenced by 2025; that year has now passed, and the real number is not known precisely. They argued that storing and analysing the data would become as big a challenge as producing it, which is why the bioinformatics part of this course matters.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: What can we do with it?
text:
What can we do with it?





Non-invasive prenatal testing: fetal DNA in the mother’s blood is sequenced
The film Gattaca (1997) imagined genetic profiling at birth, less than 30 years ago



NIPT panel: Shendure et al. (2017) DNA sequencing at 40, Nature 550:345 (© Springer Nature)


Sequencing has moved into the clinic. In non-invasive prenatal testing, the small amount of cell-free fetal DNA in the mother’s blood, which mostly comes from the placenta, is sequenced to screen for chromosomal conditions; a positive screen is confirmed with an invasive test. Gattaca, from 1997, imagined a society that sorts people by their genome at birth. That was less than 30 years ago. It is worth discussing where the line should be.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
From sample to library


The extraction method decides what is possible later: purity, fragment length, RNA integrity
Long reads need high-molecular-weight DNA: no vortexing, no PCR; HiFi sheared to 15–20 kb, ultra-long not sheared


Library preparation turns your sample into molecules the sequencer can read. Extraction quality matters: fragment length and purity limit what you can do later, especially for long reads. The DNA is fragmented to the size the platform reads, adapters are added, usually with sample barcodes called indexes, and often a short PCR follows. For long reads we avoid PCR, and shear only gently: PacBio HiFi libraries are sheared to 15 to 20 kb, while ONT ultra-long protocols skip shearing altogether.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Fragmenting DNA


There are three common ways to fragment DNA. Mechanical shearing with sonication or focused acoustic energy, for example Covaris, gives random breaks but needs an instrument. Enzymatic fragmentation uses an endonuclease mix: fast and cheap, with a small sequence bias. Tagmentation, next slide, fragments the DNA and adds adapters in one step.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Tagmentation


Tagmentation uses a modified Tn5 transposase loaded with two adapter sequences. It cuts the DNA and pastes the adapters onto the ends in one step. A short PCR then adds the sample indexes and the flow-cell binding sequences. It replaces four steps of classic library prep. Illumina’s version is now called Illumina DNA Prep, formerly Nextera DNA Flex; there the transposomes sit on beads, which makes fragment size less sensitive to how much DNA you put in. Because each fragment gets a random pair of the two adapters, some fragments end up with the same adapter at both ends; those do not amplify properly and are lost.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
From RNA to a library


For RNA-seq, the first choice is which RNA to keep, because 80 to 90 percent of total RNA is ribosomal. Poly-A selection catches mRNA by its tail with oligo-dT beads; it needs intact RNA. rRNA depletion removes ribosomal RNA with probes; it keeps non-polyadenylated RNA and works on degraded samples such as FFPE. The RNA is fragmented and copied to cDNA. In a stranded library the second strand is made with dUTP and destroyed, so each read tells which strand the gene was transcribed from. After that, adapters, indexes and PCR are as for DNA.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Read types


Single-end sequencing reads one end of each fragment. Paired-end reads both ends, so we know the two reads are a fixed distance apart, which helps mapping and finding structural variants. Long reads cover a whole molecule in one go. Unique molecular identifiers are random tags added before PCR; reads with the same UMI come from the same original molecule, so PCR copies can be collapsed, which matters for quantification. Mate-pair libraries and 10x Genomics linked reads, discontinued in 2020, have been replaced by long reads and Hi-C.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Illumina: sequencing by synthesis


The library molecule has flow-cell binding sites, P5 and P7, and sample indexes. On the flow cell each molecule is copied about a thousand times in place, forming a cluster in a nanowell. Then each cycle adds all four nucleotides, each with a removable block so the polymerase adds exactly one base, and labelled so that each base gives its own signal; in two-colour chemistry G carries no dye at all. The instrument images the flow cell, the colour of each cluster gives its base, the dye and block are cleaved, and the cycle repeats, for example 2 times 150 cycles.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Illumina sequencing by synthesis
Watch the following video to understand Illumina’s sequencing by synthesis:
▶ Overview of Illumina Sequencing by Synthesis Workflow
Illumina, on YouTube

Video: © Illumina, Inc.


Click the link to open Illumina’s own animation on YouTube. It shows standard SBS chemistry: cluster generation by bridge amplification, then cycles of nucleotide addition, imaging and cleavage. The NovaSeq X works the same way in principle but uses patterned flow cells with exclusion amplification and the newer XLEAP chemistry. Opens in the browser.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
This is how it looks



Lanes are imaged tile by tile
Each spot is one cluster; colour = base in this cycle
Early flow cells: clusters at random positions. Today: patterned nanowells, billions of clusters



A flow cell is a glass slide with lanes. The camera images it tile by tile, and each tile shows thousands of clusters as coloured spots. On early, non-patterned flow cells, clusters grow at random positions. Current patterned flow cells put the clusters into a regular grid of nanowells; a 25B flow cell holds billions of clusters. With exclusion amplification, free adapters left in the library can cause slightly more index hopping, between 0.1 and 2 percent of reads; unique dual indexes let you filter those reads out.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Improvements: two-colour chemistry


Figure: own work, CC BY 4.0; colour encoding: Illumina Knowledge article 000008422


Most current Illumina instruments use two images per cycle instead of four. In the original two-colour chemistry of the NextSeq 500 and NovaSeq 6000, A is bright in both channels. In XLEAP-SBS, used on the NovaSeq X, NextSeq 1000 and 2000 and MiSeq i100, C is the base seen in both channels, A only in blue, T only in green. In both, G is dark. That saves time, but a cluster that has stopped working is also dark and is called G. This is why reads from NextSeq and NovaSeq often end in long runs of G, which have to be trimmed. The older 4-channel and the iSeq’s 1-channel chemistry follow the same idea with different encodings.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: Third generation: single molecules, long reads
text:
Third generation: single molecules, long reads









PacBio HiFi
Oxford Nanopore




How
Polymerase copies a circular template, watched in real time
Strand pulled through a protein pore, current is measured


Length
15–20 kb
As long as the molecule, up to > 1 Mb


Accuracy
Typically Q30 (99.9%)
~Q26 (99.75%) per read



Both: no PCR needed, and methylation is read directly from the native molecule.






Note



Q20 = 1 error in 100 bases
Q30 = 1 in 1,000
Q40 = 1 in 10,000.

Accuracy: manufacturer specifications (PacBio 2024, Oxford Nanopore 2025)




Third-generation platforms read single molecules without amplification. PacBio watches a polymerase copy a circular template many times, which gives HiFi reads that are both long and very accurate. Oxford Nanopore pulls a single DNA or RNA strand through a protein pore and reads the change in electric current. Note: ONT is strand sequencing; the older ‘sequencing by cleavage’ idea was abandoned. Both detect base modifications such as methylation directly.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
PacBio: single-molecule real-time sequencing



A polymerase sits at the bottom of a zero-mode waveguide
Dye on the phosphate: a flash per added base, then the dye is cut off
Revio: 25 million wells per SMRT Cell



The key part is the zero-mode waveguide, a well so small that light only reaches its bottom, where a single polymerase sits. Each nucleotide carries its dye on the phosphate. When the polymerase incorporates a base, the dye flashes in the light, and it is cut off with the phosphate, leaving natural DNA. A Revio SMRT Cell has 25 million of these wells.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
PacBio HiFi: accuracy from repetition


Figure: own work, CC BY 4.0. Revio SPRQ-Nx: ~$345 list, < $300 at scale per HiFi human genome (PacBio press release, 26 May 2026)


The template is a SMRTbell: double-stranded DNA closed by hairpin adapters into a loop. The polymerase goes round and round, so each molecule is read many times. Single passes have random errors, but because they are random they cancel out in the consensus, giving HiFi reads of 15 to 20 kb. HiFi is defined as at least 99 percent accurate, Q20, and most HiFi bases reach Q30. The Revio with the new SPRQ-Nx chemistry, shipping since May 2026, lists about 345 dollars per human HiFi genome and under 300 at scale; Vega is the benchtop version.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Oxford Nanopore


Figure: own work, CC BY 4.0. Accuracy: nanoporetech.com/platform/accuracy (accessed Oct 2026)


A motor protein unwinds the DNA and feeds one strand through a protein pore in a membrane, at about 400 bases per second. Ions flow through the pore, and each group of bases in the pore blocks the current in its own way. A neural-network basecaller, Dorado, turns this current trace, the squiggle, into bases. With R10.4.1 pores and Kit 14, ONT reports a modal single-read accuracy of 99.75 percent with its most accurate basecalling model; duplex mode reads both strands for higher accuracy. The same signal reveals methylation, and RNA can be read directly.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: Long reads for RNA: whole transcripts
text:
Long reads for RNA: whole transcripts


Most genes make more than one transcript isoform. With short reads, a read inside a shared exon fits every isoform, so isoforms have to be inferred statistically; only reads in the parts that differ, an exon used by one isoform only or a junction that skips it, tell them apart. Long reads cover the whole transcript, so each read shows directly which isoform it came from. PacBio Kinnex and Iso-Seq sequence full-length cDNA; ONT can sequence cDNA or the native RNA itself, which also reveals RNA modifications such as m6A.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: Short fragments can take over a long-read run
text:
Short fragments can take over a long-read run


Figure: own work, CC BY 4.0. Idea after a post on the Albertsen lab blog (Aalborg University; no longer online)


The same mass of DNA contains far fewer long molecules than short ones. One microgram of 350 bp fragments has about 2.6 times 10 to the 12 molecules; one microgram of 100 kb fragments only about 10 to the 10. So a small amount of short DNA by mass can dominate by molecule count. Example: if 1 percent of the mass is 1 kb fragments and 99 percent is 100 kb, about half of all molecules are short, and short molecules get sequenced too. Idea after the Albertsen lab blog.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: Getting long DNA: pulsed-field gel electrophoresis
text:
Getting long DNA: pulsed-field gel electrophoresis





Gentle extraction: high-molecular-weight DNA
Fragments > 15–20 kb run together on a normal gel: use pulsed-field gels
Remove short fragments: gel-based (BluePippin, cut-off ~10–15 kb) or bead-based kits



Long reads need long DNA. Extraction has to be gentle: no vortexing, wide-bore tips. On a normal agarose gel, everything above 15 to 20 kb runs together, so pulsed-field gel electrophoresis, which switches the field direction, is used to check size. To get rid of short fragments, which would otherwise take a large share of the reads, you can size-select on a gel-based system such as BluePippin, or use bead-based short-read eliminator kits.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Read-length distributions and N50

N50: half of all bases are in reads at least this long.

Simulated data. Figure: own work, CC BY 4.0


Long-read runs are summarised with N50: half of all sequenced bases are in reads at least this long. Counted by reads, most reads are fairly short; counted by bases, most of the data sits in the long reads. Here the median read is 8 kb, but the N50 is almost 18 kb. Always check which of the two a report shows.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Which platform for which question?












Illumina NovaSeq X
Element AVITI
PacBio Revio (HiFi)
Oxford Nanopore




Read length
2 × 150 bp
2 × 150 bp
15–20 kb
As long as the molecule: ~100 bp to > 1 Mb


Accuracy
Q30+
Q30+ (Q40+ with UltraQ)
Q20+, typically Q30
Q20–Q26 per read (duplex Q30)


Best for
Large cohorts, RNA-seq counts, lowest cost per base
Very accurate short reads
Genome assembly, phasing, full-length isoforms
Longest reads, structural variants, direct RNA, field work




Short reads are cheap and plentiful, long reads span repeats and whole transcripts.

Manufacturer specifications, 2024–2026


A rough guide. Illumina is the default for counting: RNA-seq expression, large cohorts, and anything where cost per base matters. Element AVITI gives very accurate short reads. PacBio HiFi is the choice for genome assembly, phasing and full-length isoforms. Oxford Nanopore gives the longest reads, structural variants, direct RNA, and works in the field. Accuracy values are manufacturer specifications.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
section: Typical errors and where they come from
text:
Typical errors and where they come from





Homopolymers. AAAAAAA miscounted → false insertions or deletions. Worst on ONT.
Not in FastQC: shows up in variant calls






GC bias. GC-rich or GC-poor regions get fewer reads.
FastQC: per sequence GC content






Poly-G and adapters. “No signal” is called G; short inserts read into the adapter.
FastQC: adapter content → trim







Duplicates. PCR copies inflate coverage. Normal for highly expressed genes.
FastQC: sequence duplication levels






Index hopping. Reads land in the wrong sample.
Prevent with unique dual indexes






Artefact or biology? Think of the technical explanation first.
→ QC lecture and today’s exercises





Höjer et al. (2026) NAR Genom Bioinform 8:lqag053; Illumina and Oxford Nanopore technical notes


Each error type matters for analysis, and most of them show up in the FastQC and MultiQC reports you will look at in today’s exercises. Homopolymer errors create false insertions and deletions; they do not show in FastQC but in variant calls. GC bias leaves GC-rich regions such as promoters and first exons with few reads. Poly-G tails and adapter read-through stop reads mapping and are trimmed by fastp or Trim Galore. Duplicates inflate counts, but in RNA-seq highly expressed genes naturally give many. Index hopping puts reads into the wrong sample. Always think of the technical explanation before the biological one.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
What’s new in 2026

Roche AXELIOS 1 / SBX (June 2026): DNA copied into a ~50× longer polymer, read through a nanopore; same-day genomes claimed (research use)
Ultima UG 200 (Feb 2026): open spinning wafer instead of a flow cell; twice the output of the UG 100, half the run time
Element VITARI (H2 2026): high-throughput instrument, up to 10 billion reads per run; ~$100 genome claimed
PacBio SPRQ-Nx (May 2026): HiFi human genome ~$345 list, < $300 at scale; adds 5hmC


Roche release 29 Jun 2026; Ultima (GEN, 23 Feb 2026); Element 2026 roadmap; PacBio release 26 May 2026 (all manufacturer claims)


Four developments worth knowing. Roche launched its AXELIOS 1 instrument with SBX, sequencing by expansion, in June 2026, for research use: DNA is copied into a surrogate polymer about 50 times longer and read through a nanopore, with same-day genomes claimed. Ultima’s UG 200, launched in February 2026, keeps the open spinning wafer of the UG 100 with twice the output and half the run time. Element plans VITARI, a high-throughput instrument claiming a 100-dollar genome, for the second half of 2026. PacBio’s SPRQ-Nx chemistry brings HiFi genomes under 300 dollars at scale. All of these are manufacturer claims, not independent benchmarks.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Sequencing in Sweden: NGI

Illumina NovaSeq X: short reads at scale
Element AVITI / AVITI24: accurate short reads, in situ
PacBio Revio: HiFi long reads
ONT PromethION: ultra-long reads, direct RNA

National Genomics Infrastructure (SciLifeLab): Stockholm and Uppsala nodes. Ask them for advice on study design before you sequence: ngisweden.scilifelab.se

NGI Sweden methods and technologies pages (accessed Oct 2026)


If you sequence in Sweden, you will probably work with the National Genomics Infrastructure at SciLifeLab, with nodes in Stockholm and Uppsala. NGI runs most of the platforms in this lecture, so you can choose by question rather than by what is available. They also advise on study design before you sequence; use that.

title: High-Throughput Sequencing
text:
Learn more


Shendure J et al. (2017) DNA sequencing at 40: past, present and future. Nature 550:345–353
Satam H et al. (2023) Next-generation sequencing technology: current trends and advancements. Biology 12:997 (open access; correction: Biology 2024, 13:286)
Marx V (2023) Method of the year: long-read sequencing. Nature Methods 20:6–11
Höjer P et al. (2026) Whole-genome sequencing with AVITI and NovaSeq X Plus reveals comparable performance with contextual biases. NAR Genom Bioinform 8:lqag053
Stephens ZD et al. (2015) Big Data: Astronomical or Genomical? PLoS Biol 13:e1002195
Goodwin S et al. (2016) Coming of age: ten years of next-generation sequencing technologies. Nat Rev Genet 17:333



These are good starting points. Shendure and colleagues give the history and outlook. Satam and colleagues is an open-access overview of current technologies. Nature Methods named long-read sequencing Method of the Year 2022; Vivien Marx’s feature explains why. Höjer and colleagues is the Swedish platform comparison. Goodwin and colleagues is the classic review, now partly historical.

title: The command line
text:
1. Get a terminal
You need a terminal that runs the Bash shell, and the exercise data.

macOSWindowsLinux


Terminal is already installed. Open it with Spotlight (Cmd + Space, type Terminal) or from Applications → Utilities → Terminal.
Newer Macs start the zsh shell, not Bash. Check which one you have:
echo $SHELL
If it says /bin/zsh, type bash and press Enter each time you open the terminal. Most commands work the same in both shells, but this way your terminal matches the exercises.


To get a terminal with a linux shell, install the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). Follow the instructions in the link above.
Very short summary:

type in the bottom left search bar “powershell”, right-click on the result and select “run as administrator”
copy-paste in the window you opened the following command:

wsl --install

reboot your system
launch WSL (the first time will take a while), set a username and a password (you will be prompted autmatically)







NoteUsing WSL (Ubuntu on Windows)?





Your Windows Desktop is at /mnt/c/Users/<your Windows name>/Desktop, not at ~/Desktop. Adjust the paths in the exercises.





Open the Terminal app. It runs Bash by default.




Download the exercise data

Download shell-lesson-data.zip.
Move it to your Desktop.
Unzip it there, so that you have a folder shell-lesson-data on your Desktop. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All…. Double-clicking can create a folder inside a folder with the same name.



Check that it works
Open the terminal and type:
cd
ls Desktop/shell-lesson-data
You should see exercise-data and north-pacific-gyre. If you get No such file or directory, ask a teacher.

title: The command line
text:
2. Exercises
We follow the Software Carpentry lesson The Unix Shell. The data is the zip you downloaded above, so you can skip the lesson’s own setup page.






ImportantTo do for you



Work through these episodes. Type every command yourself, do not copy and paste. Do the challenges and only then open the solutions.

Introducing the Shell
Navigating Files and Directories
Working With Files and Directories
Pipes and Filters

Skip the sections about Nelle (“Nelle’s Pipeline: …”). They come at the end of the episodes.








TipPay extra attention to




Paths. Before each command, ask yourself: where am I (pwd), and where is the file I want? Most errors on the server later are a wrong path.
nano and touch in episode 3. You will write your own scripts with nano on the server. Do the challenge Creating Files a Different Way, which uses touch.
rm is permanent. There is no bin to get files back from.




Bonus

If you finish early, try your hand at Shell Scripts: save commands in a file and run them. On the server, every job you submit is a script like this. Skip the Nelle section. Some challenges use loops from episode 5; you can skip those.







NoteNeed a reminder?



The Carpentries reference page lists all commands from the lesson. explainshell.com explains any command you paste into it.

title: The command line
text:
3. Discussion
We will talk about these questions in class.

You type cd data and get No such file or directory, but you are sure the folder exists. What could be wrong, and which commands help you find out?
When would you use an absolute path, and when a relative one? Which one still works if you move your project folder?
Why do many bioinformaticians avoid spaces in file and folder names?
What can you do in the terminal that is hard to do by clicking in a file browser? And the other way round?
